Learning Objectives
List the applications for musculoskeletal ultrasonography.
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of ultrasonography.
Identify applications for diagnostic and interventional ultrasonography.
Basic Information
Terms
Specific terminology is used in ultrasonography to describe the images and artifacts.
Echogenicity, echotexture


Terms
The currency of ultrasonography is the echo. Structures can be echogenic if they reflect
sound (bone, calcification, foreign bodies) or echolucent if they let sound pass through
(fluid). Echogenic structures appear white and bright, and echolucent structures appear
black and dark.
Anisotropy

Anisotropy
Anisotropy is the quality of a structure with certain structural alignment (such as nerves
and tendons). This quality may lead to artifacts, depending how the manner in which the
structures are aligned relative to the ultrasonography beam (Resource 1). Anisotropy
occurs if the ultrasonography beam is not perpendicular to the structures of interest,
typically tendons, ligaments, and nerves. With anisotropy artifact, a tendon may appear
falsely hypoechoic, simulating a tear. The anisotropy can be resolved by correcting the
angle of the transducer (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Grayscale ultrasonographic images of a volar wrist at the level of the carpal
tunnel. A, Cross-sectional image of the flexor carpi radialis tendon (arrow), observed
adjacent to the carpal tunnel, is normal in appearance. Note that the adjacent flexor
digitorum superficialis/profundus tendons (bracket) within the carpal tunnel appear
hypoechoic (darker) because of anisotropy. B, Image obtained with the angle of the
transducer corrected shows that the tendons (bracket) appear more hyperechoic

(brighter). (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
General Principles
Ultrasonography involves the use of high-frequency sound waves to produce images.1
Image resolution is determined by the length and frequency of waves1,2-4 (Figure 2;
Resources 2, 3, and 4).
The technique of Doppler ultrasonography can be used to image blood flow. Doppler can be
used to evaluate for deep vein thrombosis, detect hyperemia related to inflammation, and
assess for vascularity in soft-tissue masses (ie, pseudoaneurysms or vascular malformations or
hemangioma). Doppler also is used for vascular mapping5,6 (Figures 3 and 4; Resources 5 and
6).
Figure 2 Ultrasonographic images of a volar wrist. A, Grayscale image shows a partially
thrombosed pseudoaneurysm (bracket). B, Color Doppler image shows the yin-yang sign (red
and blue vascularity demonstrating bidirectional flow). A vessel contiguous with the
pseudoaneurysm also is observed. (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Figure 3 Ultrasonographic images of an ulna without (A) and with (B) Doppler show a
lobulated, heterogeneously hyperechoic to hypoechoic mass within the subcutaneous soft
tissues, demonstrating vascularity. Biopsy revealed a hemangioma. (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011

MD, New York City, NY.)
Figure 4 Doppler ultrasonographic image of a tibial nerve shows a heterogeneously
hypoechoic and lobulated nerve sheath tumor (brackets) with some vascular flow; however,
the lesion is contiguous with the tibial nerve (arrows) rather than the vessel. (Courtesy of
Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)

General Principles
A technique that developed from Sonar technology used during World War I,
ultrasonography involves the use of high-frequency ultrasound waves applied through a
probe placed on a patient’s skin7 (Resource 7). The probes are available in various sizes
and shapes for different applications.
Higher frequency ultrasonography (eg, 8 to 18 MHz hockey stick) involves a short
wavelength and is ideal for producing higher resolution images of superficial structures
(ie, tendons of the fingers) or superficial nerves (ie, the superficial peroneal nerve or the
median nerve at the carpal tunnel). Lower frequency ultrasonography (eg, 6 to 15 MHz
or 9 MHz linear probe) involves a longer wavelength and is better for assessing deeper
structures (ie, imaging the hip joint or the iliopsoas tendon), depending on a patient’s
size and the depth of the structure of interest.
Other Techniques
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
4/42


Other Techniques
Other techniques, such as elastography, the use of contrast, image registration across
modalities, and three-dimensional imaging are used less commonly. Elastography can be
used to assess the elasticity of soft tissues and currently is used in research studies to
assess changes in the elasticity of tendons in tendinopathy.1 Contrast can be used to
evaluate capillary blood flow. Image registration can be used to guide procedures, and
three-dimensional imaging is commonly used to show parents images of their in utero
fetuses.
Advantages and Disadvantages
Advantages
No ionizing radiation
Portable
No true contraindications
High resolution 
Dynamic and interactive
Cost

Advantages
Ultrasonography results in high-resolution images and is ideal for imaging small and
superficial structures, such as superficial nerves. Dissimilar from CT and radiography,
ultrasonography produces no ionizing radiation; therefore, it can be used in imaging
children and pregnant women without concern.1 Ultrasonography machines can be
quite small and portable, making them accessible in many scenarios. Larger
ultrasonography machines are less portable but produce higher-quality images. Patients
who may not be able to undergo MRI because of claustrophobia or safety concerns can
undergo ultrasonography.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
5/42

The imaging modality is performed in real time and patients can be asked about areas of
pain, patients moved around to evaluate for impingement, and areas can be stressed
(eg, to look for joint opening in patients with a collateral ligament injury). These qualities
make ultrasonography effective for guiding needle interventions. Ultrasonography also
typically is less costly than MRI and CT.
Disadvantages
Operator dependent
Limited field of view
Need acoustic window
Patient needs to cooperate.
Requires direct contact

Disadvantages
Ultrasonography is performed in real time by an individual operator, who takes images
as the study is being performed. Ultrasonography relies on the operator identifying the
correct structure and accurately documenting the findings.
The ultrasonography probe is small and must be passed over the area of concern;
therefore, large areas or multiple areas require a great deal of time to image in detail. CT
and MRI can cover large areas more easily.
The ultrasonography beam needs to be able to access the area of interest. Superficial
structures are the easiest to visualize. Structures within joints (such as the cruciate
ligaments) or deep in the body are more difficult to evaluate. Although ultrasonography
may be able to image cartilage at the margins of the joints, it cannot be used to assess
the entirety of cartilage.The quality of ultrasonography may be limited in patients with
obesity, particularly if deeper structures need to be evaluated. In addition, scarring and
metal may result in shadowing and obscure the evaluation of structures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
6/42

Because ultrasonography is interactive, imaging may be difficult in uncooperative or
pediatric patients. For some joints, specific positions and dynamic maneuvers often are
required to obtain high-quality images. A patient’s ability to cooperate with appropriate
positioning may be limited by pain or decreased range of motion. Lastly, direct contact
may be painful or difficult in patients with open wounds or very tender lesions.
Indications
Superficial Structures

Superficial Structures
Ultrasonography can be used to evaluate most superficial structures. Deeper structures
also are amenable to ultrasonography if they are not very deep or located below bone,
lungs, or bowel gas. Structures amenable to ultrasonography include tendons,
ligaments, nerves, soft-tissue masses, and superficial bones such as ribs or metatarsals.
Shoulder

Shoulder
Ultrasonography is an excellent imaging modality for evaluating the shoulder. It is as
accurate as MRI in evaluating the rotator cuff. It is limited in evaluating the labrum and
cannot be used to evaluate the glenohumeral joint for cartilage loss.
Elbow

Elbow
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
7/42

Ultrasonography can provide a comprehensive assessment of the lateral and medial
epicondyles, ulnar collateral ligament injury (with dynamic imaging), the ulnar nerve, and
the biceps and triceps tendons.
Hand and Wrist

Hand and Wrist
Ultrasonography often is requested to evaluate for synovitis and erosions in the hands.
It also is beneficial for the evaluation of tendons, ligaments, pulleys, and nerves.
Hip and Pelvis

Hip and Pelvis
Ultrasonography is used for the evaluation of superficial findings, such as trochanteric
bursitis and abductor tendon pathology, and pathology of other tendons around the hip,
including the hamstrings and adductors.
Pediatric Hip

Pediatric Hip
Ultrasonography is an excellent method for evaluating the unossified femoral head in
infants with hip dysplasia. It also is an easy and accurate imaging modality to assess for
effusions in older children.
Foot and Ankle
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
8/42


Foot and Ankle
Ultrasonography frequently is used to evaluate the tendons around the ankle and toes.
Forefoot neuromas, tarsal tunnel, and plantar fascia also are evaluated readily via
ultrasonography.
Nerve

Nerve
High-resolution evaluation of any superficial nerves is possible via ultrasonography.
Foreign Bodies

Foreign Bodies
Ultrasonography is the best imaging modality for identifying foreign bodies not observed
on radiographs. The objects do not have to be radio-opaque.
Soft-Tissue Masses

Soft-Tissue Masses
Ultrasonography often is the initial imaging modality used for palpable soft-tissue
masses and can provide an accurate delineation of superficial soft-tissue masses.
Occasionally, ultrasonography alone may help the surgeon reach a diagnosis in patients
with a nerve sheath tumor and some patients with a lipoma.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
9/42

Vascular Imaging

Vascular Imaging
Ultrasonography is the standard imaging modality for the evaluation of deep vein
thrombosis in the legs (outside the pelvis) and the arms. Vascular mapping and
evaluation of stenosis is another field in which ultrasonography is effective.
Fractures

Fractures
Superficial fractures, such as in the ribs, can be visualized via ultrasonography.
Image-Guided Procedures

Image-Guided Procedures
Image guidance makes procedures performed with the use of a needle safer and more
accurate. Ultrasonography is an excellent method to guide joint and bursal aspiration
and injection; tendon sheath injection; needle barbotage of tendons; soft-tissue biopsy;
hematoma, seroma, or cyst aspiration; tendon and fascial release; nerve injection and
blocks; aspiration of calcific tendonitis; and several other procedures. Some surgeons
are beginning to use ultrasonography to guide percutaneous pedicle screw placement
(Figures 5 and 6).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
10/42

Figure 5 Grayscale ultrasonographic images of a shoulder. A, Longitudinal axis view
shows a normal supraspinatus tendon (arrows) with a curvilinear, fibrillated pattern. B,
Short-axis view shows a cross-section of the fibrillary bundles of the supraspinatus
tendon (arrows). The white bracket indicates the full width of the tendon. (Courtesy of
Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Figure 6 Grayscale ultrasonographic images of the proximal humerus of a patient who
underwent subpectoral biceps tenodesis. A, Hyperechoic suture material (arrow) is
observed within the biceps. B, A cortical defect (arrow) is observed along the proximal
humerus. (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Ultrasonographic-Guided Procedures

Ultrasonographic-Guided Procedures
Ultrasonography may be used during the therapeutic injection of steroid or other
substances, such as platelet-rich plasma. Therapeutic injection with cortisone can be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
11/42

performed for pain relief; however, variability exists in the range of relief patients
experience. Joint, bursal, tendon sheath, perifascial, and perineural injections also may
be performed. Adverse effects and complications of cortisone injection include flare
reaction, infection, and tendon or fascia rupture. Diagnostic injection of anesthetic can
be used to immediately evaluate symptomatic relief and pinpoint a patient’s source of
pain.
Ultrasonography also may be used for guidance during the aspiration of hematomas or
fluid collections to evaluate for infection; however, very congealed or clotted hematomas
may not be amenable to percutaneous needle aspiration, even with the use of a large-
gauge needle. Lastly, depending on location, soft-tissue masses may be biopsied under
ultrasonographic guidance. (Figure 7).
Figure 7 Grayscale ultrasonographic image of a forearm with a soft-tissue mass shows
reverberation artifact deep to the biopsy needle (arrows). The bracket indicates the
extent of the hemangioma. (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Limitations of Ultrasonography for Biopsy

Limitations of Ultrasonography for Biopsy
Ultrasonography is not ideal for bone biopsy. Bone biopsy is better performed under CT
guidance because ultrasonography cannot penetrate well into bone, and the throw of
the biopsy needle cannot be visualized. Ultrasonography may be difficult to perform in
the hands and wrists or the feet given the limited tissue available to stabilize the biopsy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
12/42

needles, particularly if important tendons or neurovascular structures are in close
proximity because it may not always be feasible to avoid important structures (eg, a
small mass near the median nerve at the wrist). In addition, in very small lesions, not
enough tissue sample may be obtained via needle biopsy (Figures 8 and 9). Depending
on patient body habitus and the depth of the lesion, very deep lesions and their
surrounding structures may not be visualized well via ultrasonography.
Figure 8 Grayscale ultrasonographic images of a forearm show a mass that was biopsied
via ultrasonographic guidance. A, Transverse axis view shows the median nerve and the
adjacent artery (yellow arrow) on one side of the mass (bracket) and the ulnar nerve
(white arrow) along the other side. Although the mass appears very large, the images are
magnified; the mass was 1.5 × 2.7 cm. B, Longitudinal axis view shows no vessels or
nerves in the way. (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Figure 9 Grayscale ultrasonographic images of an upper arm with a mass. A, Transverse
axis view shows the biopsy needle in the center of the lesion. B, Longitudinal axis view
shows needle biopsy (arrows) of the mass (bracket), with the transducer placed in the
center to avoid biopsy of the adjacent nerves. The mass was an enlarged lymph node.
(Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Foreign Bodies

Foreign Bodies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
13/42

Echogenic structures that do not appear hyperdense on radiographs can be identified
via ultrasonography; however, visualization may be difficult if adjacent air, scarring, or
edema is present. Typically, a small, focused region of interest is important in evaluating
for small foreign bodies. Tiny shards of glass also may be visualized via ultrasonography;
however, but visualization may be difficult if adjacent air is present (Figure 10).
Figure 10 Grayscale longitudinal (A) and transverse (B) axis ultrasonographic images of a
plantar foot show a splinter (arrows) embedded within the plantar soft tissues between
the third and fourth metatarsal heads. The splinter appears hyperechoic on the
ultrasonographic images but was not visible on radiographs. Note the difficultly
distinguishing the splinter from the surrounding echogenic foci in the short axis.
(Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Fractures

Fractures
Fractures can be observed in superficial locations, such as the ribs or the fifth metatarsal
(Figure 11).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
14/42

Figure 11 Ultrasonographic images of a foot with a fracture of the fifth metatarsal base.
A, Cortical disruption of the fifth metatarsal base (arrow) with surrounding mild
hyperemia is observed rather than a continuous, smooth bright cortex. B, AP radiograph
demonstrates corresponding ultrasonographic probe positioning. (Courtesy of Susan C.
Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Synovitis

Synovitis
Ultrasonography may be useful as a quick examination to evaluate for joint effusions in
children, whether from transient synovitis, inflammatory synovitis, or infection (septic
arthritis/osteomyelitis). However, the presence of a joint effusion and/or synovitis is a
nonspecific finding (Figure 12).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
15/42

Figure 12 Grayscale ultrasonographic images of the hips of a 2-year-old patient with
right-sided hip pain. A, Image of the unaffected left hip shows normal hypoechoic, thick
cartilage overlying the ossified femoral head capital epiphysis. B, Image of the right hip
shows a cortical irregularity of the proximal femoral metaphysis (white arrow) and the
capital head epiphysis. A small joint effusion is observed anteriorly, with thickened
synovium (yellow arrow). Visualization of joint fluid is dependent on the size of the
effusion; unless a joint effusion is large, visualization deep to the anterior cortex of bone
is difficult, and joint effusion may not be visualized on ultrasonographic images. In
addition, the hip joint cannot be visualized via a posterior approach on ultrasonographic
images because of the overlying muscle and fat. (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New
York City, NY.)
Ultrasonography of the Shoulder
Ultrasonography is sensitive and specific for the evaluation of many structures in the shoulder.
Ultrasonography can be used to evaluate the rotator cuff tendons and the long head of the
biceps tendon, pre-operatively and post-operatively. 
Bursitis or synovitis also can be identified via ultrasonography

Ultrasonography of the Shoulder
Ultrasonography can be used to assess the rotator cuff before and after repair, as well
as the long head of the biceps tendon. It also can be used to evaluate for subacromial
subdeltoid bursal thickening, fluid distension, and glenohumeral joint effusion. However,
ultrasonography can penetrate only the superficial portion of the joint, and a joint
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
16/42

effusion may not be visualized well unless it is large. Similarly, ultrasonography is not
ideal for evaluating the labrum or cartilage because these structures cannot be
visualized in their entirety. Lastly, ultrasonography may be used for image guidance
during injections, such as an acromioclavicular joint injection3,8 (Resource 8).
Rotator Cuff

Rotator Cuff
Tendons should appear slightly hyperechoic (bright, white), with a fibrillar pattern
(Figure 5). In patients with tendinosis, the fibers of the supraspinatus tendon appear less
distinct, with hypoechoic areas. The tendon also may appear thickened (Figure 13). Fluid
appears anechoic (black) on ultrasonography, and a fluid-filled gap indicates a tear
(Figure 14). Sutures may be observed as curvilinear hyperechoic structures within the
tendon (Figure 15).
Figure 13 Images of a rotator cuff. A, Longitudinal axis ultrasonographic image of the
shoulder shows tendinotic supraspinatus tendon fibers, which have become thickened
and less distinct. B, Coronal proton density MRI shows ultrasonographic probe
positioning to obtain an ultrasonographic image in which the supraspinatus tendon is
visualized in the longitudinal axis. Placement of the probe along the superolateral
shoulder with the patient in a neutral position will capture only a small portion of the
supraspinatus tendon insertion onto the greater tuberosity. To visualize the entire
supraspinatus tendon, the patient should be asked to position the arm as if reaching for
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
17/42

his or her back pocket, with the elbow pointed posteriorly (Crass position). (Courtesy of
Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Figure 14 Longitudinal axis ultrasonographic images of two different rotator cuffs. A,
Image of a rotator cuff with an intact subscapularis (bracket). B, Image of a different
rotator cuff shows a subscapularis with a full-thickness tear, with an anechoic, fluid-filled
gap (brackets). (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Figure 15 Ultrasonographic images of the rotator cuff of a patient who underwent
rotator cuff repair. A, Longitudinal axis view shows echogenic suture anchors (arrows) at
the greater tuberosity. B, Transverse axis view shows a fluid-filled re-tear of the
supraspinatus tendon (arrows). (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011

Biceps Tendon

Biceps Tendon
Similar to any tendon, the long head of the biceps tendon should have a slightly
hyperechoic, fibrillated appearance in the longitudinal axis. In the short axis, it should
have a rounded or slightly ovoid appearance because it is in cross-section. It can be
followed distally to the level of the pectoralis major tendon insertion; however, the intra-
articular course of the biceps tendon proximally is not visualized well on
ultrasonography (Figures 16 and 17). Ultrasonography can be used to evaluate for
tendinosis or tears of the biceps tendon (Figure 18).
The retractors used during biceps tenodesis may cause stretch injury of the nerves. The
nerve most injured is the musculocutaneous nerve (0.6% during subpectoral tenodesis),
followed by the axillary, radial, medial, and ulnar nerves, respectively. Nerve injuries are
more common with the subpectoral technique than with the suprapectoral technique9
(Figure 6; Resource 9).
Figure 16 Images of a biceps tendon. A, Short-axis grayscale ultrasonographic image
shows the long head of the biceps tendon (bracket) within the bicipital groove, with trace
anechoic fluid deep to the tendon. The tendon has a somewhat fibrillated, hyperechoic
appearance. B, Axial proton density MRI shows ultrasonographic probe positioning along

(arrow). (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Figure 17 Grayscale longitudinal axis ultrasonographic image of a biceps tendon shows

Glenohumeral Joint, Subacromial Subdeltoid Bursa

Glenohumeral Joint, Subacromial Subdeltoid Bursa
The subacromial subdeltoid bursa, if collapsed, should appear as a thin echogenic
curvilinear structure overlying the rotator cuff tendons. If inflamed, the bursa may
appear thickened and distended by fluid (Figure 19).
Only a small portion of the glenohumeral joint can be visualized via ultrasonography; the
entirety of the joint can be visualized via MRI or CT. The surface of the bone creates an
artifact known as acoustic shadowing,10 which is characterized by only darkness beneath
the cortical bone (Figures 20 and 21; Resource 10).
Figure 19 Grayscale ultrasonographic image of the glenohumeral joint of a patient with
subacromial subdeltoid bursitis. The bursa appears thickened (arrows outline the
superficial portion of the bursa), with anechoic fluid. (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New
York City, NY.)

21/42

the joint capsule (arrows) and a small portion of the labrum (asterisk). The hypoechoic to
anechoic structure deep to the joint capsule may appear similar to a joint effusion but

flipped to mimic on the orientation of the ultrasonographic image. (Courtesy of Susan C.

Ultrasonography of the Elbow
Lateral Epicondylitis/Tennis Elbow
Ultrasonography can be used to evaluate the medial collateral ligament of the elbow. 
Radial and ulnar nerves also can be assessed via ultrasonography because these structures
are well visualized. 
Ultrasonography is a quick imaging modality to determine the presence of elbow joint
effusion. 
Lateral epicondylitis can be identified as a thickened common extensor origin, with or without
a tear. 

Lateral Epicondylitis/Tennis Elbow
The common extensor origin is observed as continuous, longitudinal bands of parallel
tendon fibrils comprising the tendons of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB),
extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, and extensor carpi ulnaris. Fibers of the ECRB
account for most of the articular portion, whereas the extensor digitorum accounts for
most of the superficial portion.
In lateral epicondylitis, the common extensor origin may have a thickened appearance
with decreased echogenicity and a loss of the normal fibrillary pattern. In addition,
associated hypoechoic tears, bony changes at the lateral epicondyle attachment, or
mineralization within the tendon may be observed3,11 (Figure 22; Resource 11).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
23/42

Figure 22 Images of an elbow. A, Grayscale longitudinal axis ultrasonographic image
shows thickening of the common extensor tendon (arrows), with irregularity and
enthesopathic changes at its insertion onto the lateral epicondyle. The radiocapitellar
joint also is observed. B, Coronal proton density MRI shows ultrasonographic probe
positioning for imaging the common extensor tendon (arrows). (Courtesy of Susan C.
Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)
Medial Collateral Ligament

Medial Collateral Ligament
The medial collateral ligament is comprised of anterior, posterior, and transverse
bundles. The anterior bundle is the main stabilizer preventing valgus instability of the
elbow, extending from the inferior surface of the medial epicondyle to the sublime
tubercle of the ulna, reinforcing the capsule.11,12 (Figure 23; Resource 12). Similar to
tendon tears, ligament tears also result in a hypoechoic to anechoic appearance of the
ligament, with disruption of the normal echogenic fibrillary pattern (Figure 24).

9/4/26, 9:59 AM
AAOS | Ultrasonography
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004011
24/42

Figure 23 Grayscale longitudinal axis ultrasonographic image of an elbow shows the


Radial Nerve
At the level of the elbow, the radial nerve divides into the superficial radial nerve, which
runs along the deep surface of the brachioradialis muscle, and the posterior
interosseous nerve (deep branch), which runs through the radial tunnel.13 The radial
tunnel consists of the joint capsule posteriorly; the brachioradialis muscle, the ECRB
muscle, and the extensor carpi radialis longus muscles laterally; and the brachialis
muscle and the biceps tendon medially.13 The posterior interosseous nerve dives within
a fat plane between the two heads of the supinator muscle belly. Entrapment of the
posterior interosseous nerve may be observed at the level of the radial head between
the brachioradialis muscle and the joint capsule, at the arcade of anastomosing
branches of the radial recurrent artery, at the ECRB muscle, within the supinator muscle,
at the arcade of Frohse, and at the leash of Henry. Entrapment most commonly occurs
at the Arcade of Frohse13 (Figure 25, Figure 26, Figure 27; Resource 13).

posterior interosseous nerve (arrow) within the fat plane just as it dives between the two
heads of the supinator muscle belly. The nerve has a normal appearance. (Courtesy of
Susan C. Lee, MD, New York City, NY.)

Ulnar Nerve

Ulnar Nerve
The ulnar nerve is located along the posteromedial aspect of the elbow joint and runs
through the cubital tunnel. Distally, it can be observed between the humeral and ulnar
heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris.14 In cross-section, the ulnar nerve should have a
honeycomb-like appearance, with hypoechoic round fascicles and hyperechoic
surrounding fat.
Dynamic imaging can be used to evaluate for ulnar nerve subluxation. The ulnar nerve is
imaged throughout elbow flexion and extension. In patients with ulnar nerve
subluxation, the nerve shifts out of the cubital tunnel, and a snap may be felt by the
patient and the examiner (Figure 30).
Figure 30 Grayscale transverse axis ultrasonographic image of an ulnar nerve (arrows) at
the cubital tunnel shows enlargement from neuritis. (Courtesy of Susan C. Lee, MD, New
York City, NY.)

Ultrasonography can be used to assess for knee joint effusion or synovitis. 
Deeper structures, such as the meniscus and cartilage, are not ideally visualized via
ultrasonography.
Typically, only the suprapatellar recess of the joint and the superficial ligaments can be
visualized via ultrasonography.

Ultrasonography of the Knee
The deeper structures (the menisci, cartilage, and cruciate ligaments) cannot be well
visualized because the distal femur, patella, and proximal tibia cortices block the
ultrasonographic beams from penetrating deeper into the joint (Figures 31 and 32). Only
a small portion of the body segments of the menisci can be visualized via
ultrasonography.

Ultrasonography of the Ankle
The ankle has many superficial structures that can be evaluated via ultrasonography. 
Ultrasonography can be used to easily assess for Achilles tendon tears, and the adjacent sural
nerve. 
The joints of the foot and ankle also can be assessed for joint effusions. 
Achilles Tendon

Achilles Tendon
The Achilles tendon, similar to all tendons, should have a fibrillary pattern. The tendon
should have a flat or concave anterior margin on the transverse axis. The retrocalcaneal
bursa also can be imaged via ultrasonography if it contains fluid or is inflamed15
(Figures 33 and 34; Resource 15).

Ultrasonography of the Wrist
Ultrasonography can be used to assess the tendons and nerves of the wrist, namely the
median nerve/carpal tunnel. 
Diseases, such as Dupuytren disease, also can be visualized via ultrasonography. 
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
The carpal tunnel canal is narrowest at the level of the hook of the hamate. The
transverse carpal ligament forms the volar margin of the carpal tunnel, attaching radially
to the scaphoid and the trapezium and ulnarly to the pisiform and the hook of the
hamate17 (Resource 17).
The median nerve may be thickened and enlarged in patients with carpal tunnel
syndrome. Ultrasonography can be used to confirm the diagnosis (Figures 36 and 37).

Dupuytren Disease

Dupuytren Disease
Palmar fibromatosis or Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative disorder characterized
by the formation of subcutaneous fibrous nodules along the palmar fascia of the hand
that form cord-like attachments to the adjacent flexor tendon. On ultrasonography, the
condition appears as hypoechoic subcutaneous nodules and cords superficial to the
flexor tendon. The length of the lesion typically is greater than the width18 (Figure 38;
Resource 18). The spiral cord in Dupuytren disease consists of the following diseased
fascial components: pretendinous band, spiral band, lateral digital sheet, and the
Grayson ligament19 (Resource 19).

Ultrasonography of the Hip
Typically, ultrasonography is used to evaluate patients younger than 6 months. 
A normal alpha angle is greater than 60°. 
Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
The unossified femoral head capital epiphysis appears hypoechoic on ultrasonography,
with small punctate foci of increased echogenicity. As the epiphysis begins to ossify, a
small central hyperechoic focus, representing bone, may be observed. Ultrasonography
typically is used as the primary imaging modality to evaluate patients younger than 6
months; after this age, the femoral head capital epiphysis typically is ossified.
The alpha angle—the angle between the ilium and the acetabular roof—is measured in
the coronal plane. Normally, this angle should be greater than 60°. Evaluation of
acetabular coverage, including evaluation for subluxation or dislocation of the femoral
head, also should be performed, as recommended in the modified Graf Classification
Scale20 (Resource 20). The beta angle also is measured in the coronal plane via a line
through the vertical ilium and the cartilaginous acetabular labrum. A beta angle greater
than 55° is abnormal. Normally, the femoral head should have more than 50% coverage
by the acetabular roof (Figures 39 and 40).
Developmental hip dysplasia is observed more often in females. Risk factors include
being first born, breech birth, a family history of developmental dysplasia of the hip, and
oligohydramnios. Unmanaged developmental dysplasia of the hip may lead to an
abnormal gait; leg-length discrepancy; osteoarthritis; and rarely, osteonecrosis.


Summary
Musculoskeletal ultrasonography is a powerful and versatile imaging modality with many
diagnostic and therapeutic indications. The imaging modality is user dependent and
difficult to interpret without training. Although somewhat limited in the United States,
the use of ultrasonography is becoming more widespread. Orthopaedic surgeons must
become familiar with ultrasonography so it can be used to its full capacity.
